Issued at 330 AM CDT Sat Aug 8 2026

Through Tonight:

A regional surface analysis taken at 0800Z depicted a cold 
front extending from just east of Wisconsin's Door Peninsula 
southwestward towards the Quad Cities. This front will continue
to drift southeastward through the remainder of this morning 
before stalling out across central Illinois and Indiana this 
afternoon. Sufficient low/mid-level moisture has resulted in the
presence of an elevated modestly unstable layer rooted near 
800-850 mb along and ahead of the front, and isentropic upglide
has taken advantage of that to support the presence of isolated
showers and a few storms across the frontal zone. This already 
sparse convective coverage should diminish further over the next
few hours as the magnitude of the ongoing isentropic ascent 
weakens with time, so will carry slight chance PoPs through a 
little past sunrise to account for any festering isolated 
shower/storm activity near the front.

Also monitoring the potential for fog this morning -- primarily
across our southern counties, where a few AWOS sites have 
already reported some visibility reductions. Think that the 
mid- and high-level cloud cover ahead of the front should be
able curtail things enough to keep the fog from getting too out
of hand and prevent a repeat of yesterday morning's dense fog, 
but will continue to monitor observational trends closely.

Most, if not all, of our forecast area should find itself north
of the aforementioned front come mid-afternoon and along the 
northern periphery of a surface ridge. As a result, dry 
conditions with more comfortable humidity levels should be 
experienced today -- particularly with northward extent -- 
amidst primarily low-mid 80s high temperatures. Mid-upper 70s 
highs are forecasted in the immediate vicinity of Lake Michigan,
where a lake breeze is expected to sharpen by early this 
afternoon. Skies today should be mostly clear outside of any 
diurnal cumulus, though they could have a milky look to them 
later on in the day as smoke originating from wildfires in the 
Pacific Northwest spreads over the area once again.


Sunday through Friday:

Tomorrow, the stalled frontal boundary will lift back northward
as a warm front, ushering evapotranspirationally-enhanced 70s 
dew points back into the area. The return of this muggy air mass
will set the stage for a prolonged, convectively active period 
of weather across the region that will begin on Sunday and 
continue well into next week. However, confidence in forecast 
specifics regarding the thunderstorm potential during this 
period inherently remains low given the involvement of a muggy 
summertime air mass and subtle forcing mechanisms, as well as 
the influence of one convective cycle on the next and the 
subsequent domino effects that follow.

The initial wave of convective activity that we'll need to keep
an eye on will develop well to our west and northwest tonight 
as a shortwave ripple embedded within stout west-northwesterly 
flow aloft acts upon the northeastern periphery of the inbound 
EML plume. It's not yet clear at this time whether this activity
will evolve into an MCS or whether it will remain disorganized 
as it propagates towards the east-southeast. At any rate, this 
activity could reach northern Illinois as early as Sunday 
morning, so that is when mentionable PoPs and thunderstorm 
chances are first introduced into our going forecast. The 
influence of this initial round of convection and the associated
cloud debris on destabilization efforts puts into question 
where and when additional convection may develop later on in the
day on Sunday.

Assuming that the air mass that will be in place doesn't get 
convectively overturned to a significant degree by this initial 
activity, a strengthening low-level jet and another subtle 
shortwave diving into the Midwest suggest that storms are likely
to redevelop somewhere in the general region late Sunday 
afternoon or evening. With northern Illinois and northwest 
Indiana appearing to be favorably positioned relative to these 
atmospheric features, would think that it is more likely than 
not that we'll see some degree of thunderstorm activity across 
our forecast area in this late day through Sunday night time 
frame, so have largely kept the higher PoPs brought in by the 
NBM for this time period. While the specific details regarding 
Sunday's thunderstorm threat remain uncertain, increasing 
instability and strengthening deep-layer wind shear will support
the potential for severe thunderstorms with damaging winds and 
hail. The moist air mass will also support torrential rainfall 
rates with any storms, so some threat for flash flooding could 
also materialize somewhere in the region.

With the muggy air mass and primary frontal zone not likely to 
budge much by Monday, Monday will similarly be a day that will 
be favorable for thunderstorms with threats for severe weather 
and flash flooding in the region. Forecas
